newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Agricultural futures take root in emerging markets.
newsitem.headline: Agricultural futures take root in emerging markets.

text.p: Futures exchanges trading in farming commodities are sprouting across emerging markets as the dismantling of agricultural controls gathers pace.

Although the new exchanges have started off small with only a handful of products traded on each, contracts in new commodities are constantly being investigated as more markets are freed from government regulation.

These findings emerged at the inaugural meeting of the Association of Emerging Agricultural Futures Markets held in Johannesburg this week, attended by representatives from Argentina, Hungary, Malaysia, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

Delegates said governments increasingly saw supply and demand as the most efficient way to allocate resources and farmers were warming to futures markets, using them to hedge out the price swings and risks associated with free markets.

John Wixley, general manager of operations at the South African Futures Exchange (Safex), said agricultural futures trade was likely to grow in southern African as the region moved towards a free trade area and foreign aid was reduced.

"Zimbabwe, Zambia, Kenya and Tanzania are all in the process of deregulating their domestic marketing systems...In the medium term, the prospects for increased use of agricultural futures to hedge price risk...look promising," Wixley said.
Ian Goggin, head of the Zimbabwe Agricultural Commodity Exchange, proposed the setting up of a regional futures exchange in southern Africa.

"Most countries in southern Africa do not have the wherewithal at this time to establish their own exchanges...I think certainly in the foreseeable future we will be looking at a regional futures exchange, maybe through Safex," Goggin said.

Safex last year set up an agricultural markets division which runs futures contracts in beef, potatoes, and white and yellow maize. Both beef and potato markets are virtually free, while internal maize trade was deregulated in 1995.
It is investigating contracts in wheat, wool and tobacco, the latter in conjuction with Zimbabwe, Wixley said.

Other emerging markets which have recently launched trade in farm futures include Hungary which in 1989 set up the Budapest Commodity Exchange to fill the gap left by the collapse of the former central planning system, the meeting heard.
The first such exchange to be launched in Central Eastern Europe, the privately-owned bourse runs contracts in maize, sunflower seed and livestock.

Argentina in 1990 began trading futures and options on maize, wheat, sunflower and soybeans. Guillermo Desiervi of the Mercado a Termino de Buenos Aires said volumes on the exchange had grown at a rate of 80 percent per annum since its launch.

In the Far East, Malaysia has well-established futures contracts in palm oil, and Kuala Lumpur Commodity Exchange acting head Raghbir Bhart said the 16-year-old exchange was now considering plywood futures and palm oil options.
The establishment of futures markets has not been without teething problems and in some cases contracts have been a dismal failure, delegates said.

Bhart said the Malaysian exchange had had to scrap trading in cocoa, palm kernels, tin and rubber after they failed to spark interest for reasons ranging from depressed prices and the availability of active and liquid markets elsewhere.

Wixley said South Africa's futures market was experiencing a number of hurdles including a lack of liquidity, difficulties in educating industry about the futures market and continued state interference in product markets.
